Dental Implants · Cost & Insurance

How Much Does a Dental Implant Cost — and How Your Insurance Network Can Save You $1,000+

By Dr. Ramin Foroughi, Periodontist October 2026  ·  6 min read

"How much will this cost?" is one of the first questions patients ask about dental implants, and it's a fair one. Implants are an investment. But the price you actually pay depends on more than the procedure itself. One of the biggest factors is something most patients never think to ask about: whether your periodontist is truly in-network with your dental insurance.

Here's what goes into the cost of an implant, and how choosing an in-network office can save you well over $1,000.

What Does a Dental Implant Cost in California?

A complete single-tooth implant includes three parts: the implant (a titanium post placed in the jawbone), the abutment (the connector), and the crown (the visible tooth). In California, the total for all three commonly falls between about $4,000 and $8,000 per tooth, with a statewide average of roughly $5,700.

Your cost can be higher or lower depending on:

  • Whether you need a bone graft or sinus lift to build enough bone to support the implant
  • Whether the tooth still needs to be extracted, and whether the socket is preserved at the same time
  • Imaging, such as a 3D CBCT scan used to plan the implant precisely
  • Sedation, if you choose nitrous oxide, oral or IV sedation
  • Your insurance: your plan's coverage, your annual maximum, and, most importantly, whether your provider is in-network

"We Accept Your Insurance" Is Not the Same as "In-Network"

This is the part most patients don't know. Many offices say they "accept" your insurance. Usually, that means they'll send the claim to your insurance company for you. It does not mean they have a contract with your plan.

An in-network (or "participating") provider has signed a contract with your insurance company and agreed to its contracted fee schedule, the discounted prices your plan has negotiated for each procedure. An in-network office can't charge you more than those contracted fees. Whatever is above that amount, the office writes off.

An out-of-network office has no such agreement. It can charge its full fee. Your plan pays its share based on its own allowed amount, and you're billed for the difference. This is called balance billing. Out-of-network offices may also ask you to pay the full amount up front and wait for your insurance company to reimburse you.

So two offices can both "take" your insurance, and you can still pay very different amounts.

How In-Network Care Can Save You Over $1,000

Here's a simplified example for implant surgery alone. The numbers are illustrative; real fees and coverage vary by plan.

  • The office's full fee for implant surgery: $3,000
  • Your plan's contracted (in-network) fee for the same procedure: $2,000
  • Your plan covers implants at 50%

At an in-network office

The office can only charge the contracted $2,000. Your plan pays 50% ($1,000), and you pay $1,000.

At an office that "accepts" your plan but is out-of-network

The office charges its full $3,000. Your plan still pays 50% of its allowed amount ($1,000). You pay the remaining $2,000.

That's a $1,000 difference on a single procedure. Add a bone graft, an extraction, or the abutment and crown, and the gap usually grows. Many implant cases also use up most of a plan's yearly maximum (often $1,000–$2,000), so staying in-network makes sure those insurance dollars go further.

How to Check If an Office Is Really In-Network

Before you schedule, ask these questions. A good office will answer them without hesitation:

  • "Are you a contracted, in-network provider with my specific plan?" Use your plan's exact name, not just the company. Some insurance companies have more than one network (Delta Dental, for example, has both PPO and Premier networks).
  • "Will you charge me only the plan's contracted fees?"
  • "Can you give me a written estimate showing what insurance is expected to pay and what I'll owe?"
  • Double-check your insurance company's provider directory or call the member number on your card.

It's also worth asking about your plan's waiting periods, annual maximum, and whether it has a "missing tooth clause," which can limit coverage for replacing a tooth lost before your coverage started.
